newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian doctors devise "pacemaker" for impotence.
newsitem.headline: Italian doctors devise "pacemaker" for impotence.

text.p: Doctors said on Wednesday they had devised a "pacemaker" which could help to cure the growing problem of impotence in men living in the developed world.
Doctors presenting the two by three centimetre (0.8 by 1.2 inch) box which is inserted into the scrotum said they had already been flooded with requests for the new breakthrough.

"In Europe, the implantable prototype will be possible within a year," said Giuseppe Tritto, director an andrology centre in Paris which helped develop the device. "We're already getting plenty of requests."
The "pacemaker" consists of a battery-operated microchip in a box that connects to sensors at the base of the penis to help men who cannot achieve an erection.
Tritto said the smart chip stimulated nerves and regulated the flow of blood through vessels in the penis, triggering a normal erection when the man was stimulated sexually.
The device, fitted during a two-hour operation requiring a small incision, would be invisible to the naked eye.

It would be worn permanently but its batteries would have to be replaced every few years. The doctors estimated it would cost around $6,500 -- similar to the cost of a heart pacemaker -- and could be on sale after five years.
Impotence is a growing problem, particularly in developed countries.
Tritto and other French and Italian andrologists -- the equivalent of "male gynaecologists" -- say men aged between 50 and 70 were most at risk, but even youths could suffer.

Swedish men might find the device of particular interest. The doctors said impotence affected 22 percent of men in Sweden, compared with 15 percent in the United States, 14 percent in France and 11 percent in Italy.
The doctors said impotence had a physical cause such as circulatory problems, diabetes, drug abuse or high alcohol or cigarette consumption in 80 percent of cases.
Stress or anxiety caused the problem far less. But they said the condition was curable in 75 percent of cases.
The "pacemaker" will be tested next year in Paris on some 15 men of varying ages suffering from impotence related to diabetes or neurological problems.
